parts: Lesson 12: Performing Arts: Music, Dance and Drama — Summary

Art is the aesthetic expression of the characteristics of the human mind – emotions called 'ras' (the ultimate satisfaction of aanand). Nine rasas (navras): Hasya (laughter), Bhayanak (fear), Rudra (anger), Karun (pathos), Veer (courage), Adbhut (wonder), Vibhatsa (disgust), Shaanti (peace), Shringaar (love/decoration). Sketching, painting and sculpture are visual arts; singing, dancing and acting are performing arts. Performing arts educated the masses, spread religion and social reform and are now also entertainment. Festivals like Lohri are celebrated with Bhangra and Giddha; many songs and dances began with fertility rites. Notes of music: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni.

The earliest tradition of music goes back to the Sama Veda, whose slokas were set to music and chanted with prescribed pitch and accent; the earliest text on performing arts is Bharata's Natyashastra (between 2nd century BC and 2nd century AD) with six chapters on music; Matanga's Brihaddeshi (8th–9th century AD) first named and discussed ragas; Sarangadeva's Sangita Ratnakara (13th century) mentions 264 ragas; ancient texts mention flute, drums, veena and cymbals; Samudragupta, King Bhoja and Someshvara patronised music and Samudragupta is shown playing the veena on coins; Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century) has songs set in ragas on the love of Radha and Krishna; Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabharati; the Saivite Nayanars and Vaishnavite Alvars set psalms to music. In the medieval period Sufis (qawwali in khanqahs) and Bhakti saints (kirtan, bhajan – Kabir, Mirabai, Surdas, Chandidas, Tulsidas, Vidyapati) encouraged music; Amir Khusrau, Baz Bahadur and Rupmati (new ragas), Ibrahim Adil Shah II (Kitab-i-Nauras), Tansen and Baiju Bawra of Akbar's court; Babur, Humayun, Akbar and Swami Haridas; Pundarika Vittal wrote Ragamala.
Hindustani, Carnatic, modern and folk music

Classical music has two traditions: Hindustani (North; traced to the Delhi Sultanate and Amir Khusrau; descendants of Tansen; styles Dhrupad, Dhamar, Thumri, Khayal, Tappa; ragas Bahar, Bhairavi, Darbari, Yaman, Megh Malhar, etc.; instruments sitar, sarod, santoor, sarangi, pakhawaj, tabla, flute, shehnai; gharanas – hereditary linkage of musicians in the guru-shishya parampara: Gwalior, Kirana, Jaipur) and Carnatic (South; composers Shyama Shastri, Thyagaraja and Mutthuswami Dikshitar between 1700 and 1850, Purandaradasa; main compositions are kritis, devotional; accompanied by flute, veena, nadaswaram, mridangam, ghatam; Carnatic alapana is similar to alap and tillana to tarana; both stress tala). With British rule violin and clarinet were adopted and orchestration, cassettes and music institutions replaced the master–disciple system. Folk music represents the emotion of the masses and marks every event: Mand (Rajasthan), Bhatiali (Bengal), Ragini (Haryana), Gulraj (Kashmir), Pandvani (MP), Sojkhwani during Muharram, carols.

The Rig Veda mentions dance; the bronze Dancing Girl of Harappa shows dance in the Indus culture; Shiva as Nataraja symbolises the creation and destruction of the cosmic cycle; temples show dancers. Classical dances: Kathakali, Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Manipuri, Kuchipudi, Odissi (also Mohiniattam). Temple dance had a religious object and court dance was entertainment. Bharatanatyam and Mohiniattam developed in temples of the south; Yakshagana (a form of Kathakali in Kerala) tells stories of the Ramayana and Mahabharata; Kathak and Manipuri are mostly related to Krishna and his leela; Odissi is related to the worship of Lord Jagannath; Kathak moved to the courts and was promoted by Muslim rulers (not Aurangzeb); Wajid Ali Shah began the Lucknow gharana (Birju Maharaj). Folk dances: Bihu (Assam), Garba (Gujarat), Bhangra and Giddha (Punjab), Bamboo dance (Mizoram), Koli (Maharashtra fishermen), Dhumal (Kashmir), Chhau (Bengal); martial dances: Cholia (Uttarakhand), Kalaripayattu (Kerala), Thang-ta (Manipur). Bharata's Natyashastra divides dance into nritta (pure footwork, pada sanchalan), nritya (anga sanchalan, expression) and natya (abhinaya, drama).

Drama's origin is traced to the Vedas; the Ramayana mentions women's drama troupes and Kautilya's Arthashastra mentions musicians, dancers and shows; drama could begin with a child's mimicry. Bharata wrote the Natyashastra and the plays Asura Parajaya and Amrit Manthan; for him drama was the perfect means of communication, with nat and nati, music, dance, instruments, dialogue, themes and stage and an enclosed theatre; the shailoosh were professional drama companies and kushilavas professional singers of heroic tales. Bhasa wrote 13 plays (Swapnavasavadatta); Patanjali's Mahabhashya mentions Kamsavadha and Balibandha. In Buddha's and Mahavira's age drama spread religion. Sanskrit was used, with women and low-class characters speaking Prakrit; Kalidasa's Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Malavikagnimitra, Vikramorvashiyam; Bana Bhatta's Harshacharita; Vidyapati introduced Hindi and regional songs. Folk theatre in local dialect: Jatra and Kirtania Natak (Bengal), Bidesia (Bihar), Raas, Jhumar, Dhola Maru (Rajasthan), Raas, Nautanki, Swang, Bhand (UP), Bhavai (Gujarat), Lalit and Tamasha (Maharashtra), Kathakali and Yakshagana (South); props dhol, kartal, manjira, khanjira. Wajid Ali Shah patronised drama. Modern theatre began when a Russian, Gerasim Lebedev, founded a Bengali theatre in Calcutta; Shakespeare influenced Indian drama; stages got rolling curtains; a Parsi company in Bombay made it commercial; Shambhu Mitra, Feisal Alkazi, Badal Sarkar, Vijay Tendulkar experimented. Types now: stage, radio, Nukkar (street plays), mono-drama, musical theatre, skits, one-act plays. Jayadeva's Gita Govinda influenced dance, drama and painting all over India. Writers: Kalidasa (Meghadutam, Abhijnana Shakuntalam), Bharatendu (Neel Devi, Satya Harishchandra, Andher Nagri), Jaishankar Prasad (Chandragupta, Ajatashatru, Skandagupta etc.).

Gandharva Mahavidyalaya, Prayag Sangeet Samiti, Indira Kala Sangeet Vishwavidyalaya (Khairagarh), Kathak Kendra, National School of Drama, Bharatiya Kala Kendra, SPIC MACAY and Sangeet Natak Akademi promote the arts; Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan and Alla Rakha run institutions abroad; ICCR and the Ministry of Human Resource Development give grants, scholarships and fellowships and arrange exchanges. The arts elevate the soul, give balance and peace of mind, self-restraint, love for all and self-confidence, helping the development of personality.
